claim: Coffee built the world's insurance industry.

knots.hatnote: It started as a monk's way to stay up for night prayers.
knots.passage: Though coffee has become a global commodity, it has a history tied to food traditions around the Red Sea. The earliest reports of coffee drinking pertain to the plant's use among the Sufis of Yemen in southern Arabia in the middle of the 15th century.
knots.fragment: The earliest reports of coffee drinking

knots.hatnote: The name on your café menu is a Yemeni port.
knots.passage: Up to the end of the 17th century, Yemen was the world's main producer for coffee, and Mocha was the world's largest shipping port for coffee.
knots.fragment: Mocha was the world's largest shipping port

knots.hatnote: Within decades, the authorities were already trying to ban it.
knots.passage: Coffeehouses in Mecca became a concern of imams, who viewed them as places for political gatherings and drinking, leading to bans between 1512 and 1524. However, these bans could not be maintained, as coffee became ingrained in daily ritual and culture among Arabs and neighboring peoples.
knots.fragment: Coffeehouses in Mecca became a concern

knots.hatnote: In London, the coffeehouse became the office.
knots.passage: Coffeehouses not only boosted the popularity of print news culture, they also helped the growth of various financial markets including insurance and stocks. Lloyd's Coffee House was where underwriters of ship insurance met to do business, leading to the establishment of Lloyd's of London insurance market and other related businesses.

payoff: A drink for staying awake at prayers ended up underwriting the world's ships.

claim: The sandwich and Hawaii were named after the same man.

recall.after: were named after the same man.

knots.hatnote: Lunch is named after an aristocrat who didn't want to stop playing cards. Allegedly.
knots.passage: It is commonly said that Lord Sandwich, during long sessions of cribbage and other card games at public gambling houses, would order his valet to bring him roast beef between two pieces of toasted bread. He was fond of this form of food because it allowed him to continue gambling while eating, without the need for a fork, and without getting his cards greasy from eating meat with his bare hands.
knots.fragment: It is commonly said that Lord Sandwich

knots.hatnote: The myth-check. His biographer thinks he was just working late.
knots.passage: The sober alternative to this account is provided by Sandwich's biographer N. A. M. Rodger, who suggests that Sandwich's commitments to the navy, to politics, and to the arts mean that the first sandwich was more likely to have been consumed at his work desk.

knots.hatnote: That work desk ran the Royal Navy, which paid for Cook's voyages.
knots.passage: Lord Sandwich was a great supporter of Captain James Cook. As First Lord of the Admiralty, Sandwich approved Admiralty funds for the purchase and fit-out of the Resolution, Adventure and Discovery for Cook's second and third expeditions of exploration in the Pacific Ocean. He also arranged an audience with the King, which was an unusual privilege for a lower ranking officer. In honour of Sandwich, Cook named the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii) after him, as well as the South Sandwich Islands in the Southern Atlantic Ocean and Montague Island in the Gulf of Alaska.
knots.fragment: Lord Sandwich was a great supporter

payoff: The man on your lunch label also has his name on a Pacific archipelago, and an Antarctic one.

claim: The man the sandwich is named after helped give us the phrase for a safe bet.

end.label: Copper-bottomed
end.description: Idiom for something sound and reliable

knots.hatnote: Same Earl, different problem: worms were eating his navy.
knots.passage: He had remarked that coppering "gave additional strength to the navy" and he reproached Lord Sandwich with having "refused to sheath only a few ships with copper" at his request, when he had since ordered the whole navy to be sheathed. The lack of coppering the navy was one of the key reasons leading to Britain losing the Thirteen Colonies.

knots.hatnote: The fix came all at once, and it came too late.
knots.passage: It was then decided that the entire fleet should be coppered, due to the difficulties in maintaining a mixed fleet of coppered and non-coppered ships. By 1781, 82 ships of the line had been coppered, along with fourteen 50-gun ships, 115 frigates, and 182 unrated vessels

knots.hatnote: Insurers noticed which ships had copper bottoms. Wikipedia still wants a source for this one.
knots.passage: As the coppering was expensive, only the better owners tended to invest in the method, and as a result the use of copper sheathing tended to indicate a well-found and maintained ship, which led to Lloyd's of London charging lower insurance premiums, as the vessels were better risks. From this stems the phrase "copper-bottomed" as an indication of quality.

payoff: “Copper-bottomed” started as an insurer's opinion of a ship's hull.

claim: Your morning coffee helped spark a revolution in the Caribbean.

knots.hatnote: One French officer and a seedling, or so the story goes.
knots.passage: Frenchman Gabriel de Clieu took a coffee plant to the French territory of Martinique in the Caribbean in the 1720s, from which much of the world's cultivated arabica coffee is descended. Coffee thrived in the climate and was conveyed across the Americas.
knots.fragment: Gabriel de Clieu took a coffee plant

knots.hatnote: The myth-check. A great story, but coffee had beaten him there.
knots.passage: According to de Clieu's account, water was rationed on the voyage, and he shared his ration with the seedlings. The story is repeated in many histories of coffee. However, a recent history points out that though it may well be true that de Clieu brought a seedling to Martinique, and perhaps even that he shared his water ration with it, coffee was already growing in the Western Hemisphere: in the French colony of Saint-Domingue since 1715 and in the Dutch colony of Surinam since 1718.
knots.fragment: water was rationed on the voyage

knots.hatnote: Saint-Domingue is now Haiti, and the coffee came at a cost.
knots.passage: Coffee was cultivated in Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, from 1734, and by 1788 it supplied half the world's coffee. The conditions that the enslaved people worked in on coffee plantations were a factor in the Haitian Revolution, and the coffee industry never fully recovered there.

payoff: By 1788, half the world's coffee came from one colony, and the people forced to grow it overthrew it.
